name: GPU prime-number range test kernel (book companion code, ch4)
listed_description: CUDA kernel where each thread trial-divides one odd candidate by odd divisors up to the square root; timed against the same loop on the CPU over three number ranges, excluding memory transfers.
claim_text: Speedup grows with range size: 1.23x, 9.66x and 67.91x; CPU 15.6056 ms against GPU 0.2298 ms for the largest range.
book_benchmark: Ranges 100,001-101,001 / 110,001 / 190,001; single-threaded CPU loop timed with std::chrono against CUDA-event kernel time; Intel Core i7-10750H and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060; compiler flags not stated; no transfers included.
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 4, section A kernel to test for prime numbers

name: GPU vector addition kernel (book companion code, ch4)
listed_description: One-thread-per-element CUDA float vector addition compared with a plain CPU loop, with and without host-device copy time.
claim_text: Kernel-only speedup reaches 44.04x at 100M elements; including copies it falls to 1.02x (212.297 ms GPU against 218.270 ms CPU).
book_benchmark: 10K to 100M floats; CPU std::chrono loop against CUDA events; i7-10750H and RTX 2060; kernel-only and with-transfer tables; flags not stated.
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 4, section Vector addition

name: Shared-memory tiled matrix multiply with unroll and fmaf (book companion code, ch7)
listed_description: 16x16 tiled CUDA matrix multiplication that stages tiles in shared memory, adds #pragma unroll and fmaf, measured against the naive global-memory kernel with Nsight Compute.
claim_text: Release build time fell from 47.33 ms to 33.37 ms, about a 42% improvement over the naive kernel in Release.
book_benchmark: Matrix kernel profiled with Nsight Compute on RTX 2060 (125x125 blocks of 16x16, so roughly 2000x2000); CMake Release (-O3) naive against all optimizations; Debug-mode runs were slower and are not the headline; one run per version, figures only otherwise.
guessed_baseline: naive one-thread-per-element CUDA matmul kernel (cuBLAS not compared)
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 7, sections Using shared memory to improve time through Putting it all together with Release configuration

name: NVIDIA cuda-samples matrixMul
listed_description: Official CUDA sample implementing tiled shared-memory matrix multiplication; the book says its own optimized kernel follows the same approach, which traces to a 2008 benchmarking paper on dense linear algebra.
book_benchmark: Not benchmarked by the book; cited only as the source of the tiling strategy.
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 7, section Using shared memory to improve time

name: GPU shared-memory tree reduction for trapezoidal integration (book companion code, ch6)
listed_description: Trapezoidal-rule kernel that sums partial results per block in shared memory with halving strides and __syncthreads, finishing the last small sum on the host; contrasted with the version that copies every partial back and sums on the CPU.
claim_text: With 1,000,000 points the plain GPU and CPU times were the same order; adding parallel reduction cut GPU time by an order of magnitude.
book_benchmark: N up to 10M doubles; speed-measurement array; CPU loop against GPU; hardware presumably RTX 2060 and i7-10750H; no table printed in the text, numbers only in the repository.
guessed_baseline: std::accumulate or sequential CPU loop; GPU version without on-device reduction
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 6, sections Calculating numerical integrals and Reducing from many

name: Two-stream chunked copy and compute overlap for vector-matrix multiply (book companion code, ch8)
listed_description: Splits a 1 GB or 4 GB matrix into row chunks, uses pinned host memory and two non-default CUDA streams so host-to-device copy, kernel and result copy overlap; compared with a no-streams build of the same kernel across chunk sizes.
claim_text: Overlap gave 25 to 31% lower execution time; best 27.05% (87.03 ms) at 1020 MB and 31.37% (343.555 ms) at 4092 MB, near 100-200 MB chunks.
book_benchmark: 16,380 x 16,380 and 32,760 x 32,760 float matrices; average of ten runs per configuration; RTX 2060 on PCIe measured near 12 GB/s; chunk sizes 273 to 16,380 rows; baseline same kernel with no streams; flags not stated.
guessed_baseline: same CUDA program without streams (copy all, then compute)
found_in: book: GPU Programming with C++ and CUDA (2025), ch. 8, section Multiplying matrices with CUDA streams, Table 8.1
